messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan, a 39‑year‑old construction worker, was still a teenager when the night the town’s historic rowhouse caught fire turned his world inside out. He had been on the crew that day, hammering nails into a porch that had been slated for renovation. The evening was unusually warm; the smell of fresh paint lingered in the air. Suddenly, a burst of orange light broke through the evening haze, and the fire's crackle cut through the quiet. Ethan’s eyes widened as the blaze consumed the wooden frame of the front kitchen, the flames licking the roof and the windows. The scream of his neighbor’s wife, her voice breaking, was a sound he would carry for years. The heat hit his face before the heat of the fire itself; he felt the hot air on his skin and smelled the acrid scent of burning wood that still lingered long after the fire trucks arrived. In the chaos he watched the neighbor’s son, a boy the same age as his younger brother, run into the house and emerge shivering, his face pale as ash. Ethan felt a sudden, unshakable sense of helplessness – that he could do nothing to stop the terror he witnessed. The memories of that night are not fleeting whispers; they come to him as vivid, isolated images. When he closes his eyes, the fire's orange blaze and the neighbor’s wife's frantic face overlay his own heartbeat. The scent of burning plaster and the taste of scorched bread that his wife had left on the counter the night before haunt him whenever he thinks about the scene. He swallows when the smell of smoke returns, the metallic taste of fear crawling to the back of his throat. This intense recall is compounded by the feeling that his senses were assaulted so strongly that the memories have become almost tangible. The memory’s clarity reinforces the belief that the world is a dangerous place where nothing can be stopped. He has come to believe that his worldview is broken. The experience shattered his fundamental assumptions about safety and competence. “The world is cruel and unforgiving,” he says, “and I can’t do anything to make it right.” The sense of helplessness, coupled with an acute sense of inadequacy, has hardened his belief that he cannot protect himself or those he loves. He insists that his anger is a threat; he suppresses it so tightly that he never allows himself to feel or express it. In the quiet hours of the night, he throws himself at a slot machine or bets on a horse race, hoping for the fleeting rush of excitement to drown the terror that gnaws at him. He deliberately tries to dissociate, to leave his body and stare at the ceiling as if it were a window to a calmer world, because he believes that feeling any emotion would bring him closer to the trauma he cannot escape. These maladaptive strategies feel like the only tools he has to keep the memories from seeping into his everyday life. When the sound of the construction site's hammering echoes across the open field, Ethan’s brain instantly flags the flashbacks. The memory surges, and the heat of that night returns, making him feel that the flames are about to ignite again. He finds himself pulling out of his shift before his supervisors notice, retreating to the truck to avoid the noise that triggers the vivid recollection. Over months, this avoidance has become routine; he misses half a day each week, missing crucial hours that he relies on for his livelihood. When he returns, his coworkers notice a tense edge, his focus broken. His partner has tried to reach out, but Ethan’s fear that his presence might attract danger keeps him distant, widening the chasm between them until their divorce became inevitable. The job has begun to feel more like a prison than a place of work, and his fear that the world is still dangerous drives him to stay away from the site, even when it is safer to be there. Ethan’s negative appraisals of the world have driven him toward these maladaptive strategies and the memories of the fire have reinforced his sense of helplessness and the belief that the world is broken. The memories, in turn, fuel his attempts to dissociate and suppress anger, further entrenching his distorted beliefs. In the first sessions, he reports relentless insomnia, waking up gasping, and a growing anxiety that the fire could return at any moment. The last month he has been unable to sleep on a normal mattress because the taste of charred wood lingers in his mouth, a constant reminder that his life remains forever tainted. The realization that he has lost a job, the end of his marriage, and the inability to share his pain with others have made him finally seek help. He fears that his anger and gambling will consume his family if nothing changes, yet he hopes that confronting the memories might free him from the endless cycle of avoidance and despair.
